topic: What if you dove to the bottom of the Mariana Trench?
research_summary: Candidates: (1) What if you dove to the bottom of the Mariana Trench? 33/40 (curiosity gap, personal stakes, huge numbers, strong visual of a descent, verifiable, not Space so it passes the variety guard; researched-queue gate 78), (2) What if all the ice on Earth melted? 30 (strong, but a documentary slot today), (3) What if you could stop time? 27 (fictional physics, weaker visual). Space & Universe is cooling down, so no space topic. Winner: the Mariana Trench dive; starts the 'The Deep Sea' cluster. Titles (/50): 'What If You Dove to the Deepest Point on Earth?' 44 (chosen); 'What If You Sank to the Bottom of the Ocean?' 41; 'Mariana Trench: The Dive' 33; '1,000x Pressure: Could You Survive?' 40; 'Diving 11 Kilometres Down' 36; 'The Deepest Place on Earth, Explained' 38; 'What the Bottom of the Ocean Does to You' 39; 'Would You Dive Into the Dark?' 37; 'The Darkest Dive' 31; 'Could Anything Live at the Bottom?' 36. Thumbnails: A the face with a tiny sub and the words 1,000x PRESSURE (chosen); B a pitch-black column with one lamp and the question 'How deep?'; C a crushed cup next to a normal cup. Hooks: 'Dive eleven kilometres down and the water presses a thousand times harder than air.' (chosen); 'No sunlight has ever touched the place you are sinking toward.'; 'Every ten metres, the sea squeezes you a little harder.'; 'The bottom of the ocean is colder than your fridge.'; 'The deepest dive ever made took four hours just to go down.' FACTS (status): Challenger Deep is about 10,935 m deep (NOAA 2021 estimate +/- 6 m; other surveys give up to about 10,994 m +/- 40 m, so the script says 'eleven kilometres') - PARTIALLY VERIFIED; pressure at the bottom is over 1,000 atmospheres (about 16,000 psi) - VERIFIED (NASA, NOAA-affiliated study, 1,000+ x sea level); over a tonne per square centimetre follows from 1,000 atm (about 1.03 kgf per cm2 per atm) - COMPUTED, stated as 'about a tonne on every fingernail' - PARTIALLY VERIFIED; bottom water about 1-4 C (2.45 C measured minimum in a NOAA-affiliated profile; Royal Museums Greenwich 1-4 C) - VERIFIED; sunlight is rarely significant beyond 200 m and absent below about 1,000 m (NOAA) - VERIFIED; amphipods swarm at depths over 10,000 m and are the snailfish's main food (JAMSTEC, Schmidt Ocean Institute) - VERIFIED; fish appear limited to about 8,000-8,500 m by the TMAO limit (hypothesis; the deepest confirmed fish is 8,336 m in the Izu-Ogasawara Trench) - PARTIALLY VERIFIED, so the script says 'fish seem to stop near eight thousand metres'; the 1960 Trieste dive took about 4 hours 47 minutes to descend (US Navy history office) - VERIFIED (one popular source says nine hours; the Navy figure is used). Left out: Vescovo's 2019 descent time (sources disagree), any claims about what a human body would feel (no gore, no unsupported physiology). Sources: https://repository.library.noaa.gov/view/noaa/33477 , https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/light_travel.html , https://www.rmg.co.uk/stories/ocean/challenger-deep-deepest-point-ocean , https://tos.org/oceanography/article/ambient-sound-at-challenger-deep-mariana-trench , https://history.navy.mil/about-us/leadership/director/directors-corner/h-grams/h-gram-041/h-041-6.html , https://www.jamstec.go.jp/e/about/press_release/archive/2017/20170824.pdf , https://schmidtocean.org/?p=2029 . Competitor/vidIQ data: NOT PUBLICLY VERIFIABLE (not queried). Risks: depth figure differs between surveys (hedged), fish-depth limit is a hypothesis (hedged). Quality gate 84/100: topic 9, curiosity 9, title 8, thumbnail 9, opening 9, story 8, visual 9, emotion 7, retention 8, series 8 - improve the emotional close, then proceed.

items: What if you dove to the bottom?

scenes.text: First, the light. Sunlight is nearly gone by two hundred metres. Below a thousand, it is pitch dark.
Then the squeeze. At the bottom, the pressure is over a thousand atmospheres. Picture a tonne pressing on every fingernail.
Is it hot down there? No. The water is just one to four degrees Celsius.
Does anything live there? Yes! Tiny shrimp-like amphipods swarm the bottom. Fish seem to stop near eight thousand metres.
Quick quiz. How long did the first dive down take, back in 1960? Four hours forty-seven minutes.
